speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POWER EFFECTS OF JAMES BAY HYDROELECTRIC PROJECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I want to say something nice about the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). I saw him as he was leaving yesterday, and he asked me if I would miss him. I said that I would but I would try to say something nice about him and that is what I am going to do now. I am going to thank him for his recitation from Desiderata the other day-I don't know what he told the caucus but he did not make them too happy. I looked up my old copy of Desiderata, and in paying tribute to the Prime Minister I would also use this as a prelude to what I am going to say and what my approach is going to be to this debate.
Speak your truth quietly and clearly and listen to others, even the dull and ignorant; they too have their story. Avoid loud and aggressive persons, they are vexatious to the spirit.
I guess we will have to put up with that. I want to say to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) that I accept his approach that the constitutional responsibility lies with a province for the steps to be taken to initiate the development of electric power. On the other hand, by our constitution, by practice and also by the statutes this parliament has passed pursuant to its right to do so, there are embodied in our laws certain restrictions on that provincial right. I am not referring to the direct
April 28, 1972

right to initiate a project but a right to attach conditions to the development of the project. I think there is no easier way to look at that than to look at what happened not long ago when the National Energy Board, a child of the federal government, acting within the jurisdiction legally given to it by this parliament, said to the producers of natural gas in the province of Alberta "You may indeed produce gas, but the limitation we place upon you is that it cannot be exported". In a mixed jurisdiction, that is the way this sort of thing operates.
In making his statement, the minister indulged in a little sophistry. I think he has been standing too close to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin), who is a master of sophistry, and a little intellectual osmosis has developed. It is true that the right to initiate any project for the development of power lies exclusively within a province but subject to the right of the federal government, or institutions developed under federal jurisdiction, to place certain obstacles or conditions which must be met before a plan can proceed and before the energy which has been developed can be exported. I do not think the minister will deny that to be the fact. Any federal government which refuses to accept that proposition and refuses to act upon it if it is considered essential, is denying its responsibility under the constitution of this country.
The hon. minister referred to the importance of this subject. It is, of course, an important subject and that is borne out by the fact that two other ministers, as well as other members on the government side, are going to speak in this debate. Then, if this is so, why did we have to wait until the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) was able to persuade the Chair that this matter was important enough that the business of the house should be interrupted for a debate? Why did the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien), the minister who has just spoken, the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis) or the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson), each of whom has some responsibility, not speak for the government or make a statement on motions? I ask them to tell the House precisely what their position is and what the government intends to do on this issue. I think they have a duty to this House in the exercise of their collective responsibility to make known to the country from time to time where they stand on important issues, and not wait until the opposition, in pursuance of its duty, drags these statements out of them.
One has sympathy and understanding, Mr. Speaker, for the desire of the Province of Quebec or any province to develop its industries, to develop its resources and to try to provide an increase in its standard of living through any of these means. It is proper for governments to do this, and I for one would never want to do anything which would interfere with the right of the Province of Quebec, the Province of Ontario and the Province of Alberta to so proceed. I think that must be the basic point of our discussion.
Today we realize more and more that our resources are not inexhaustible. We know that steps taken by governments and corporations, private or public, in the develop-
James Bay Power Project
ment of these resources can lead to consequences which may not have been foreseen originally but which may have serious detrimental effects upon future generations of Canadians. If we do not draw these consequences to the attention of the government-I am speaking not only of the federal government but of provincial governments-and make known the knowledge that we have obtained, we shall be abdicating our responsibilities with respect to development projects of this kind.
My hon. friend from Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) has objectively and reasonably put forward grounds to show that this question must be examined by parliament. I intend to deal with one aspect of the matter, that is, the responsibility of the federal government under the Navigable Waters Protection Act. I shall speak about what this government should do and what it has failed to do. While so doing I will yield to temptation and show, by illustrating what happened on another occasion, precisely how governments and the people can get into serious trouble when they neglect to abide by the provisions laid down in a particular and important piece of legislation.
I will not take up the time of the House by reciting the legislation. It is well known; it has been discussed in the House and has been the subject of questions. We know today, from answers given by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) with respect to two bridges which were constructed or are being constructed by the corporation of the province of Quebec charged with responsibility for the project, that an application has been made under the Navigable Waters Protection Act. There is another bridge with respect to which approval may not have been given. One must also consider the extent to which these bridges and other works will interfere with the free flow of the river.
I will quote a highly qualified witness to confirm the correctness of my statement regarding the necessity for complying with the Navigable Waters Protection Act in these matters. Speaking about the Moran hydroelectric development in British Columbia, the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis), on page 9 of a news release dated March 1, 1971, said as follows:
And what do I mean by that? Well, the Fraser River is a major salmon river. It is also navigable. It therefore comes under two federal acts, the federal Fisheries Act and the federal Navigable Waters Protection Act. Before a dam could be built at Moran, B.C. Hydro would have to get a permit from the Federal Department of Transport under the Navigable Waters Protection Act. And before it could begin construction it would also have to satisfy the federal Minister of Fisheries that there will be adequate provision for fish passages and so on.
The minister then quoted sections of the Fisheries Act. I agree with what he said: it is right, it is sensible and it is the law. The law must be complied with in every province of this country. It was not complied with a number of years ago in the case of the Peace River. May I recapitulate the facts.
In the early part of the 1950s a Swedish industrialist, Axel Wenner-Gren, applied to the British Columbia government for a permit with regard to the feasibility study and ultimate construction of a dam across the Peace River near Hudson Hope. He hoped that this would lead to exploration and development of natural resources in a large part of the trench of the Rocky Mountains. Ultimate-

April 28, 1972
James Bay Power Project
ly, Mr. Bennett, Premier of British Columbia, decided that there must be development of two rivers in that province, the Columbia River and the Peace River. This proposal was objected to by the Hon. Davie Fulton who was minister of justice in the government led by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). The proposal was rejected. Then the government changed.
In the new government the then secretary of state for external affairs, now government leader in the Senate, being determined to pull off a coup and produce Mr. Bennett at Washington for the signing of a treaty, permitted, nay, encouraged, the government of British Columbia to proceed with the power construction program involving the two rivers. He encouraged the province of British Columbia to build a dam across the Peace River without requesting the consent which was essential and should have been obtained under the Navigable Waters Protection Act.
At that time I was the only member of the House who was aware of the problem. I challenged the minister of justice of the day and finally, after much questioning, obtained an admission to the effect that the Navigable Waters Protection Act applied, that permission had to be obtained for construction and that application had to be made. At that time the Department of Public Works was responsible in the House for that legislation. For two years I pursued this question with the Liberal government and got nowhere.
Finally, the dam was constructed. Irreparable damage was suffered by the lower parts of the Peace River and particularly the Athabasca-Peace River delta, and no one can be certain as to the consequences to the Mackenzie River basin. The Minister of the Environment admits this. In a press release dated February 17, 1971, we find the following statement:
Mr. Davis said that preliminary hydrological studies indicate that filling of the Williston reservoir, created by the construction of the Bennett dam in B.C., appears in part responsible for reduced water levels in Lake Athabasca and ecological changes in the Athabasca delta.-
Ecologists say that a continuation of low water levels in the Athabasca delta may permanently change the vegetation and in turn the animal life. They say that it is especially necessary that high-level flood flows cover the delta not later than the spring of 1972, in order to avoid permanent ecological changes.
I thoroughly agree with that statement. I was in that area recently, and we do not know what will happen. I only hope there will not be permanent damage. The government cannot avoid its responsibilities. The waters I am talking about come squarely within the definition of navigable waters under the act. One of the last cases I was involved in before coming to this House concerned a narrow creek not wider than the aisle which separates the front benches of this House. In that case, a fisherman seeking to go from his home to Lesser Slave Lake was compelled to travel through the waters of that stream which crossed the land of a farmer. The farmer built a fence across the stream. Officials of the federal Department of Public Works in Edmonton instituted an action, secured an injunction and ultimately a judgment for damages. The farmer concerned was compelled to take down the fence.
Without doubt, the definition of navigable rivers and navigable waters as interpreted by the Exchequer Court of this country makes it clear that such rivers and waters are covered by this legislation. Nobody in the government has told us what the government's intentions are regarding the navigable waters in question. I hope, and I will give the government credit in this regard, until the contrary appears that these projects will not be allowed to proceed until the corporation of the province of Quebec charged with responsibility files plans and those plans have been examined in detail by competent and responsible engineers, so that the results which will flow from the proposed changes to the rivers will be acceptable.
That is the plea I am making. I could be much more critical, but I think this is the time for plain speaking. This is the time to urge upon the government the view of the vast majority of people in this country, namely, that when governments and powerful corporations become involved in vast public works undertakings, every precaution must be taken to ensure that the kind of irreparable damage we have experienced in the Peace River area is not perpetrated in other parts of Canada.
I urge the government to take this plea to heart. If they do not, I assure them that as long as they sit on the other side of the House they will have to deal with a determined opposition and, I am sure, with a determined people in this land.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POWER EFFECTS OF JAMES BAY HYDROELECTRIC PROJECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was in no hurry to rise but clearly the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) wants to speak after me, so I am not in the least embarrassed, quite the opposite. I do not evade committees or the House. I can face the situation as it is.
I welcome the opportunity for us to take part in this debate which is extremely important, particularly so for a certain group of Canadian citizens, the Indians of the James Bay area. In fact, it is gratifying for me to be able to clarify the matter and to give a detailed explanation of the situation of the Indians now facing this problem.
First of all, I refer to the point raised by the hon. member who spoke on behalf of the New Democratic Party. He has, concerning the Indians, an attitude which in our times is no longer acceptable, that is that we should replace them completely in all situations.

We decided a few years ago that we should not act as great white fathers to the Indians, that we would respect their wishes. I have been very much involved in this project since it began. On many occasions I have talked with ministers of the province of Quebec on behalf of the Indians, but those who speak officially for the Indians in Quebec are the Indians themselves through the band councils which have now joined together in a provincial association.
A year ago, the Association of Indians in Quebec asked me not to participate directly in this affair. They have held many discussions among themselves. Both Mr. DeLisle and Mr. Gros Louis have informed me of the

April 28, 1972

progress of their strategy. They have initiated discussions on many aspects of Indian affairs with the Quebec government. They have said all along that they wanted me to wait, to be ready to intervene when the time came. I have respected this wish.
The Indians have, of course, passed resolutions, and so on. I overheard the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) talking about a resolution passed last July. It is true that a petition was signed last July, but I tell the hon. member and the House of Commons that it was only on Monday that the association sent me officially a copy of this petition and asked me to take part in the debate.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POWER EFFECTS OF JAMES BAY HYDROELECTRIC PROJECT
speechtext: They asked you last July.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POWER EFFECTS OF JAMES BAY HYDROELECTRIC PROJECT
speechtext:
No, Sir. They passed the resolution last July but they decided not to send it to me. They decided they ought to work among themselves before making up their minds what they should do. In the meantime we have looked into the situation carefully. We recognize that it is a serious one. I said in the House when questioned this week that now the Indians have officially requested my help I am happy to offer them my assistance. They have asked me to meet them next week and I have agreed to do so.
Since the beginning of this affair I have discussed the situation three or four times with Mr. Bourassa, Premier of Quebec. I have been in touch with him this week and asked him for a meeting after the Indians meet with me next week. He said any time I want to meet him in connection with this matter he will be happy to discuss it with me. So we have been available. We are willing to help the Indians find a solution.
What will be the best solution for them? This week my assistant deputy minister, Mr. Ciaccia, had a discussion with Chief DeLisle and the representative of the Indians in the James Bay area, Chief Billy Diamond. They had a long talk on technical questions and the course to be taken. This will be followed up in the course of my meeting with the Indians next week. But I wish to repeat that I shall not decide for the Indians. I think the Indians should be left to make a choice, and I will be there to help them. They are well organized at the present time and they want a piece of the action.
Apparently members of the New Democratic Party and others are asking me to take over in a paternalistic way and stop certain things or do certain things for the Indians. I will not do that, because this government does not wish to take over responsibilities which the Indians themselves are willing to discharge.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POWER EFFECTS OF JAMES BAY HYDROELECTRIC PROJECT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POWER EFFECTS OF JAMES BAY HYDROELECTRIC PROJECT
speechtext:
We are not paternalistic toward the Indian people but, as I say, we are willing to help them. There are two courses open. There is a solution which could be negotiated. The Indians would like us to help them. They have tried alone and they have not been completely satisfied. Now they say the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development can help them. Fine. I am ready to help them. I will sit down with them and I will meet the Premier of Quebec to discuss the problems of the 6,000 Indians who could be affected by this development. It is
James Bay Power Project
my duty to do so under the terms of section 91(24) of the British North America Act and, as usual, I shall discharge my duty-but not at the expense of the self-respect, pride and wishes of the Indians of this area.
The problem, Mr. Speaker, is extremely complicated because it is common knowledge that the lands in question in the James Bay area have not always belonged to the Quebec government and have not always been under its jurisdiction. These lands, formerly known as Rupert's Land, belonged to the Hudson's Bay Company and, in 1867, the Canadian government, in a petition addressed to Her Majesty, asked the Imperial government to hand over Rupert's Land to the government of Canada.
It is in 1870 that Rupert's Land was actually handed over by the Imperial government of Her Majesty to become part of the Canadian confederation. For several years, this land was administered by the federal government and in 1898, the southern part of the Rupert's Land was transferred by the federal government to the province of Quebec.
The northern part was in effect transferred in 1912 under the transfer act of that same year, in which it was stated that the interests of Indians were to be protect ed if the area came to be developed, as has been mentioned by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Harding) who spoke for the New Democratic party.
We are quite aware of the judicial aspect of the situation in this area, and we firmly intend to protect the interests of Indians.
Does this mean, however, that in order to protect the interests of the Indians, we must act irresponsibly? The Indians recognize the complexity of this situation. They themselves are trying to discover what solution could best serve their interests.
This is why they asked me a few days ago to meet with them in order to clarify this matter, and we will meet with them next Wednesday to try and make some progress. Economic progress does not necessarily exclude the reaching of a reasonable agreement between the parties concerned.
I think the Quebec government should recognize that it is in the interest of all Quebecers to see to it that a development of this kind will not cause irreparable prejudice to Indians, and that the people who must be the first to benefit from this development should be the Indians who have been living in this territory from times immemorial.
I think it is possible to ensure that some agreement is reached which will be satisfactory to all parties concerned. Of course, the judicial situation cannot be shrugged away. It is indeed an extremely complex situation which involves various concepts. However, studies have been made on this subject by independent commissions. We are all familiar with the report of the Dorion Commission, which also recognizes that the Indian problem is important to the economic and social development of this whole area.

April 28, 1972
James Bay Power Project
The task force on the environment which studied this situation last summer also came to the conclusion that the people most deeply affected would no doubt be the Indians.
Mr. Speaker, we are ready because we have been studying the situation very carefully in the last few months. Every time questions were put in the House, I replied that we were following the debate on behalf of the Indian population without directly participating in it, but if the Indians were to request us officially to intervene to safeguard their interests in this debate, we would be ready to do so.
I must say to the House that in the course of the discussions I have had-though unofficially since the Indians were opposed to my involvement in this question-with the premier of Quebec, he has been very understanding and anxious to find a solution that would be acceptable both to Amerindians of that territory as well as to the government of Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to state once more that we will help Indians to find a negotiated settlement which will be the best thing to do since legal wranglings would certainly not be the best course of action to solve this problem.
At all events, we are going to consult with the Indians and whatever the ultimate decision they ask us to make, we will support them, in accordance with our responsibility to do so under the British North America Act of 1867.
Once again, I hope that the first citizens of the country will not be used in this debate, as has too often been the case, as an all-purpose political football. I think we should show restraint, objectivity and seek out a solution that would first of all benefit the first citizens of this country. Such is certainly our aim. I can assure my hon. friends that I have no other concern and no intention of reverting to the old paternalistic attitude whereby we, white people, should at this time intervene and systematically replace the Indians of New Quebec and James Bay at the negotiation table, speak on their behalf and jointly with them and the government of Quebec, in order to protect their interests in that territory.

I should like to pay tribute to the Indians of the James Bay area and the Quebec association for their participation in the events leading up to this debate. They have had many meetings with the provincial administration on many different topics. They have acted responsibly. They told my assistant deputy minister this week that what they want is a solution. They do not want to be stubborn; they just want to reconcile their interests, which are vital, with the interests of the Canadian public in general and particularly the citizens of Quebec. I am delighted that we can talk with them and will probably be able to find a solution. I assure them that this government will be there to help them arrive at a negotiated solution. If that does not work and if the Indians decide upon other legal courses of action, we will again be there to help them as it is our responsibility to do.
On behalf of my colleague the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) I should like for a few minutes to touch upon-

Navigable Waters Protection Act.
I realize that up to now the government of the province of Quebec has recognized that the Department of Transport has jurisdiction in that field under federal law. And at present-as stated by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin)-there has been a request for the construction of a bridge on one of the rivers involved. Of course, plans are being worked out for the construction of other bridges on other rivers. The Department of Transport has already sent inspectors in that area so they can get an idea of the work to be done.
Of course, everytime the government of Quebec submits a request to the Department of Transport the minister has assured the House-and I can do it also-that such request will be examined on its merits and according to the letter and the spirit of the law.
This legislation is intended to protect shipping and transportation on those rivers. Naturally, until now they have been very little used by shipping. That is why to this day the Minister of Transport has not had to get very much involved in the building of bridges or wharves on those rivers since they are very little used for navigation and transportation except by Indian canoes.
I think that, in this connection, the Department of Transport has discharged its responsibilities and the Quebec government has admitted the validity of the federal Navigable Waters Protection Act. Besides, this matter has never been disputed by the Quebec authorities and heaven knows how many Quebec rivers such as the Saguenay, the Saint-Maurice, the Ottawa and some others have been the subject of developments and directives from the Department of Transport.

I do not want to take up too much of the time of this House, Mr. Speaker, but I should like to just state the position of this government. It was only on Monday of this week that the Indians asked us to participate directly in the debate. We have already said to them we will have meetings with the Indian associations and representatives of the James Bay area, and those meetings will be in Ottawa next Wednesday, Thursday and Friday. We are planning to hold meetings whenever it is convenient to them, and we have agreed on Wednesday next as the date for a meeting.
Since Monday, when I received this request, and the resolutions passed by the different bands in the past weeks and months, I got in touch once more with the Quebec government and have been assured that they are willing-

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POWER EFFECTS OF JAMES BAY HYDROELECTRIC PROJECT
speechtext:
I thank you, Mr. Speaker, and I thank the hon. members for their courtesy.
I plan to meet these representatives next week and, in the days that will follow, I will be in touch with the Premier of Quebec who has already agreed to meet with me at my convenience. We are following the situation very closely, and I can assure hon. members that the interests of the Indians will be protected by this government, and that we will keep our cool. I am sure the best interests of everyone concerned will be served by finding a settlement acceptable to everyone.
I am very grateful that no one in this House so far this afternoon has taken an extreme position, denying any development or anything like that. I think this is the approach we have to follow. There are many interests which have to be considered and I want to say to the Quebec government, the Indians and members of this House, that we will make sure the interests of the 6,000 Indians living in this area will be well protected.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POWER EFFECTS OF JAMES BAY HYDROELECTRIC PROJECT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POWER EFFECTS OF JAMES BAY HYDROELECTRIC PROJECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was very interesting this afternoon to listen to the statements made so far from the government side of the House. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) took a very narrow view of a situation lying entirely within the jurisdiction of his department. I listened with interest to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) who did make reference to the problems of the Indian people. Quite frankly, while he said a lot about talking to Indians, neither he nor the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources gave us any kind of assurance that this government is going to cease doing what it has been doing, namely flaunting the laws of this parliament and the constitution of Canada as they relate to the rights of the aboriginal inhabitants of this part of Canada or, indeed, of any other part.
It is small wonder that the Indians of that particular region may have thought it advisable to talk first to the government of Quebec, in light of the announced policy of the government as made clear by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) of this country, that as far as the federal government is concerned it refuses to recognize the aboriginal rights enshrined in the constitution of this country. I certainly would not want to see the minister go back to what he referred to as "any old paternalistic attitude" in his discussions with the Indians. However, I would have liked to hear him make a positive statement assuring the members of this House and the people involved that the government of Canada was prepared to protect their constitutional rights.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POWER EFFECTS OF JAMES BAY HYDROELECTRIC PROJECT
speechtext: That is what I said.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POWER EFFECTS OF JAMES BAY HYDROELECTRIC PROJECT
speechtext:
The minister made some reference to the act of 1912, and this was mentioned by my colleague the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Harding), in which this parliament validated an agreement between the government of Canada and the government of the province of Quebec. It reads:
James Bay Power Project
That the province of Quebec will recognize the rights of the Indian inhabitants in the territory above described to the same extent, and will obtain surrenders of such rights in the same manner, as the Government of Canada has heretofore recognized such rights-
Perhaps in 1912 the government was still recognizing the necessity of obtaining surrender rights from the aboriginals, although the present government is not doing so either in the province of Quebec, the Northwest Territories or, for that matter as far as I can determine, anywhere else in this country. That is the nub of the question and that is why the minister, when he speaks in his engaging way, has to hedge and go around and around in circles, saying he must wait for resolutions from the Indian people and then have meetings and discussions with them, after they have discussed things with the Assistant Deputy Minister and officers of the department.
The minister did make some reference to the fact that the territory under discussion in this resolution was not originally part of the province of Quebec. It is interesting to note that, but I should like to suggest to him that he might have gone back to the Royal Proclamation of October 7, 1763, which sets out certain boundaries. It reads:
The Government of Quebec bounded on the Labrador coast by the river St. John, and from thence by a line drawn from the head of that river through the lake St. John, to the south end of the lake Nipissim; from whence the said line, crossing the river St. Lawrence, and the lake Champlain, in 45. Degrees of north latitude, passes along the high lands which divide the rivers that empty themselves into the said river St. Lawrence from those which fall into the sea;
Later on there was the act of 1791, which separated Lower Canada, and the Union Act of 1840 that put the pieces together again. We then moved on to the point where in 1867 the Dominion of Canada was established under the British North America Act. The point that has to be mentioned, and the minister made reference to it, is that these territories known as Rupert's Land and the Northwest Territory in 1870 were added to and became part of the new nation of Canada under the direct jurisdiction of the federal government. It is interesting to note that in the Order of Her Majesty in Council of 1870, based on the British North America Act, there is reference to a matter which I think is pertinent to the debate today. I should like to just make one or two brief references to it.
I asked the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) on a couple of occasions what the government was doing in relation to the terms and conditions under which these lands were transferred to the province of Quebec from their original territorial status so far as Canada is concerned. I also asked what position the government was taking with regard to the proposed James Bay development with particular reference to the rights of the Indian people in that region. The minister said they have been looking into the matter. When I asked the minister directly if he would participate in this debate today, he apparently decided to hide behind the skirts of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien). We have not had from the government any clear policy on this matter.
I quote as follows from term 14 of the order of 1870 of Her Majesty with regard to Rupert's Land and the Northwest Territories:

April 28, 1972
James Bay Power Project
Any claims of Indians to compensation for lands required for purposes of settlement shall be disposed of by the Canadian Government in communication with the Imperial Government; and the Company shall be relieved of all responsibility in respect of them.
In other words, that was the transfer of jurisdiction to the government of Canada. In schedule (A) of an address to Her Majesty there is an explanation of what is involved here. Schedule (A) is an address to Her Majesty the Queen from the Senate and House of Commons of Canada. It is addressed to the Queen's Most Excellent Majesty and reads:
That in the event of your Majesty's Government agreeing to transfer to Canada the jurisdiction and control over the said region, the Government and Parliament of Canada will be ready to provide that the legal rights of any corporation, company, or individual within the same shall be respected, and placed under the protection of courts of competent jurisdiction.
This is the part I wish to emphasize:
And furthermore, that, upon the transference of the territories in question to the Canadian Government, the claims of the Indian tribes to compensation for lands required for purposes of settlement will be considered and settled in conformity with the equitable principles which have uniformly governed the British Crown in its dealings with the aborigines.
That raises the question of what were the equitable principles of the British Crown. These are part of our constitutional documents. In that connection one must go back to the royal proclamation of 1763. The royal proclamation in part reads:
And We do further declare it to be Our Royal Will and Pleasure, for the present as aforesaid, to reserve under our Sovereignty, Protection, and Dominion, for the* use of the said Indians, all the Lands and Territories not included within the Limits of Our said Three new Governments-
One of these was the government of Quebec.
-or within the Limits of the Territory granted to the Hudson's Bay Company, as also all the Lands and Territories lying to the Westward of the Sources of the Rivers which fall into the Sea from the West and North West as aforesaid.
And We do hereby strictly forbid, on Pain of our Displeasure, all our loving Subjects from making any Purchases or Settlements whatever, or taking Possession of any of the Lands above reserved, without our especial leave and Licence for that Purpose first obtained.
And, We do further strictly enjoin and require all Persons whatever who have either wilfully or inadvertently seated themselves upon any Lands within the Countries above described, or upon any other Lands which, not having been ceded to or purchased by Us, are still reserved to the said Indians as aforesaid, forthwith to remove themselves from such settlements.
And whereas great Frauds and Abuses have been committed in purchasing Lands of the Indians, to the great Prejudice of our Interests, and to the great Dissatisfaction of the said Indians; In order, therefore, to prevent such irregularities for the future, and to the end that the Indians may be convinced of our Justice and determined Resolution to remove all reasonable Cause of Discontent, We do, with the Advice of our Privy Council strictly enjoin and require, that no private Person do presume to make any purchase from the said Indians, of any Lands reserved to the said Indians, within those parts of our Colonies where, We have thought proper to allow Settlement; but that, if at any Time any of the Said Indians should be inclined to dispose of the said Lands, the same shall be Purchased only for Us, in our Name, at some public Meeting or Assembly of the said Indians, to be held for that Purpose by the Governor or Commander in Chief of our Colony respectively within which they shall lie-

As the minister of Indian affairs has at least indirectly admitted today, under the British North America Act he has upon him the responsibility of acting as an agent of Her Majesty in connection with the treatment that is outlined in that proclamation which has been passed on. I submit it is inherent in the acts of 1898 and 1912 which enlarged the original boundaries of the province of Quebec. This is clearly a prior condition to any entry upon these lands for such purposes as hydroelectric development. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) suggested, and I freely admit it, that apart from this and some of the other federal areas of jurisdiction referred to here it is a matter for the province of Quebec.
I submit this government is not making clear that it is prepared to abide by the constitution of this country and see that the Indians enjoy the constitutional protections set out in some of the documents to which I have referred. That clarification we have not had so far today from a government spokesman. I submit that before any move is made this question must be clarified. Anything else will constitute trespass.
Unfortunately, because of my observations of federal government action in parts of Canada which still remain directly under their jurisdiction as far as land resources are concerned, I am not very hopeful that the Indians, when they have the forthcoming meetings with the minister to which he referred, will receive very much backing from him in negotiations with the province of Quebec. I am inclined to believe, in light of recent events, that some time since 1912 at least the rest of us in Canada have turned our backs upon the constitution and the statutes enacted by parliament.
What in fact is happening is that the government of Canada, and in many cases the governments of the provinces, are going blithely ahead in their own sweet way as if such documents did not exist. From my point of view, that is the nub of the question that must be debated and settled in this House of Commons prior to any participation by the federal government with the government of Quebec in the question of hydroelectric development in the James Bay region. That is why I am very happy that the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka brought this matter forward, especially in light of the continuing lack of any clearcut statement from the government, because it gives us an opportunity to seek, if we can, to persuade the government to fulfil its constitutional responsibilities.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jack Davis (Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Minister of the Environment
maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POWER EFFECTS OF JAMES BAY HYDROELECTRIC PROJECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I would like to thank the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) for moving this motion. Obviously, judging from the response from all corners of the House, there is not only a lively interest in the subject but also a good deal of thinking has been done about it in recent weeks and months. In his motion, he refers to three main areas of concern: one, interference with the relocation of Indians, and this matter has been dealt with by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien); two, altering the course of navigable waters protected under the Navigable Waters Protection Act, and this has been dealt with by several speakers this afternoon; and finally, three, the effect on
April 28, 1972

the total Canadian environment. It is item number 3 to which I shall be principally directing my remarks.
I think that the essence of the concern in respect of the environment relates to timing, to ecological studies, and to environmental investigations which must be carried out before the final decision to undertake large scale development and construction is made. It is a matter of timing. We should and must do our environmental engineering first before construction begins on a large scale. This principle applies to large projects as well as small ones. It must apply to projects which fall under the responsibility of all three levels of government in this country. Indeed, it must be followed in respect of all kinds of development which has measurable impact on our environment in Canada.
In the United States, and increasingly in Canada, we are insisting on the preparation of what I might call environmental impact statements. In order to prepare proper environmental impact statements, we must first obtain the basic biological data on which they can be built. We need a good deal of background information, in other words, on the living resources in an area, how they will be affected by a particular development, and what the alternatives to that development are so that we can make sure that the best possible construction proceeds and that information is available in advance of construction, as I said earlier. We are in the process of obtaining this kind of information in respect of James Bay. "We" certainly includes the province of Quebec and it includes the federal Department of the Environment.
In order to describe the sequence which we are following in respect of a project which falls much more directly under federal jurisdiction, namely, a possible pipeline or pipelines down the Mackenzie Valley, we are currently spending in the order of $15 million on studies which will require a three year period to make sure that all of the ecological data is assembled beforehand, that environmental maps are available, that all of the necessary data which bears on wildlife, fisheries, and forestry, indeed all flora and fauna, is available before the final choice, the final selection, is made by the National Energy Board. That is the sequence which we are following in respect of that project. A similar sequence is being followed in respect of the James Bay project.
The James Bay project is unique in several respects. One, of course, is its massive scale. Another is that the province of Quebec itself requested help from the federal government in respect of the assessment of the environment. This certainly did not happen in respect of the big Bennett Dam on the Peace River, a project of great scale in western Canada, the construction of which began in the early 1960's. The consequences of that project have been considerable and they have been damaging outside of the province of British Columbia. Clearly, we would have benefited considerably in western Canada had the environmental engineering preceded the decision to go ahead and build that massive project.
As I said, the province of Quebec has asked for the help of the federal government in the assessment of environmental effects. We have been supplying expertise. We have some of the world's top biologists in the employment of Environment Canada. We have several of the world's
James Bay Power Project
top authorities on wildlife and on fisheries. Canada is one of the leading nations, has done a great deal of research, and knows a great deal about the nature of its resources. In the area of forestry we have a good deal of expertise as well. We have some of the world's finest meteorologists, climatologists and some very well known oceanographers. These people have been asked to help out in the assessment of the James Bay Project. The assessment is proceeding a step at a time. I might call the assessment, a six months assessment which began in the summer of 1971, phase I.
The second assessment, which will cover a period of 18 months or more, has begun this spring. The first assessment involves quick on-the-site surveys and a thoroughgoing review of the literature. A summary report entitled "A Preliminary Study of the Environmental Impacts of the James Bay Development Project in Quebec" was released in February of this year. It was, as I indicated, the result of a joint effort by experts employed by the province of Quebec and our own experts in Environment Canada. To my surprise, and I think the surprise of many people, it did not pinpoint any substantial environmental effects which might have been characterized, for example, as likely to be catastrophic. It did, however, indicate that there were a number of areas of concern, and it did say quite emphatically that because of the lack of baseline data further investigation would have to be undertaken. Those additional investigations are under way in phase II.
Phase II, which is now under way, involves investigations particularly in the areas which might be described as climatological, which involve expertise in the area of hydrography, and also will call on the knowledge of our people who have been concerned with migratory birds. They are concerned with tides and the drift of ice as well. In order to put some of this information on the record, I should like to refer back briefly to the first task force report, a report which is published and which is already available to the public, but I might also add, which is backed up by some 50 studies, all of which are available. They are available in several universities and through several departments in the province of Quebec. They are also available in a number of departmental libraries here in Ottawa. I understand they are also available in the library of the University of Toronto. There is no secrecy here. However, we are only beginning phase II. I can say definitely that, so far as the government of Canada is concerned, we have every intention of publishing all of the studies which are prepared by our experts at the conclusion of each phase or stage in these environmental investigations.
More particularly, Mr. Speaker, I might quote from the study which includes the findings of the task force. This was written at the end of Phase I, and was published in February of this year. I quote as follows:
On the basis of limited data available, the Task Force can identify only one ecological impact of potentially alarming proportions and significance-the impact on the native population of the area.
As I said, Mr. Speaker, this matter has already been dealt with by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. The report went on to say:

April 28, 1972
James Bay Power Project
Appropriate action must be taken in advance to alleviate the ensuing disturbance in their mode of life.
There do not exist enough data to permit a positive statement to where useful action in advance must also be taken. For example, intelligent planning is required so that the destruction-of the downstream reaches of the rivers concerned, and of their ecologically sensitive estuary and bay areas can be minimized.
Quoting further:
Finally there are those impacts which are unavoidable and unalterable consequences of the James Bay development scheme, for example, flooding of forest-producing lands, loss of anadro-mous fish from one or more river channels, and some reduction in sediment and nutrients reaching sea level as a result of entrapment in upstream reservoirs.
The task force found:
There are insufficient data to support a clear-cut over-all preference between the NBR-
Meaning the Nottaway, Broadbank and Rupert proposal.
-and La Grande proposals.
Indeed, one of the terms of reference of that task force was to see which of those two major alternative schemes was preferable from an over-all environmental point of view. Apparently, the task force was unable to reach a conclusion by the spring of this year in respect to that term of reference. Again quoting:
The Task Force has found no cases of fauna or flora species that are near extinction or which are very rare and would be endangered to the point of extinction.
Again quoting:
There do not exist enough data to permit a positive statement to be made that climate in James Bay itself, or in the surrounding area, or even continentally, will or will not be measurably influenced by one or both of the hydroelectric projects now being considered.
Later, it said:
-the Task Force feels that on the geographic scale of these projects alone the effects on the ice regime and other climate-controlling factors will not be more than local.
In other words, the effects, which are likely to be minimal, would be highly localized and probably confined to the province of Quebec.

speechtext: What is the date of that report?

speakerposition: Minister of the Environment
maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POWER EFFECTS OF JAMES BAY HYDROELECTRIC PROJECT
speechtext:
The report is dated December, 1971, and it was released in early February.
The final paragraph in its conclusions section reads:
The Task Force sees that James Bay now provides, on a grand scale, an opportunity to integrate ecological research with a major engineering program in order to develop data and experience that will be needed in future resource developments in these latitudes. In this way James Bay could become a laboratory of world-wide significance.
In other words, we are embarking on something which both in scale and in consequences is in some measure unique, and considerable care is necessary in order to protect the environment.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I might refer briefly to several of the recommendations which the task force has produced, and which flow logically from the conclusions which I have already quoted. One of these recommendations is:
[Mr. Davis.}
That the James Bay project be used as a large-scale natural laboratory for comprehensive multi-disciplinary research into environmental problems and studies of how ecological processes are modified by major developments at these latitudes.
Another recommendation is:
That priority attention be given, before construction starts, to the gathering of data of existing environmental conditions to constitute a base-line measurement against which to relate subsequent changes both temporary and permanent.
And still quoting, Mr. Speaker:
That particular attention be given to river reaches below points of diversion, the estuaries into which they flow, and the storage reservoirs upstream to insure that the transition between the existing ecological equilibrium of these areas and the ultimate new equilibrium shall be as gradual and as non-destructive as possible. This means a planned control of flows and water levels during construction, particularly including maintenance of adequate minimum flows. Effective planning and action to regulate this transition process can be expected to prevent serious consequences similar to those created by the Bennett Dam in the Athabasca Delta area in Alberta.
And still quoting:
That every effort be made to completely cut as much flooded timber lands as possible.
I might say parenthetically that I believe this is the intention of the Quebec government and of Quebec Hydro. Quoting further:
That all future environmental impact studies related to the James Bay development be centrally co-ordinated so as to insure effective communication and interaction between the different scientific teams involved, to avoid duplication of effort in some areas and lack of effort in others.-
The final conclusion I will quote is:
That the co-ordinating mechanism be designed so as to (i) reflect the inter-relationships between the various identifiable elements of the total ecosystem; (ii) provide for the conduct in parallel of both short-term and long-range research studies; and (iii) recognize the jurisdictional responsibilities of the various agencies concerned and harmonize their efforts in the common task.
From what I have already said, it must be apparent to all hon. members that there has been some considerable measure of co-operation between the province of Quebec and the federal government on this matter. This is certainly to be welcomed in view of the fact that there has been very little co-operation of this kind in the past relative to large hydroelectric projects anywhere in the country, so that in one very important sense we are breaking new ground. There has been very close and, I believe, very effective liaison between the new ministry of the environment in Quebec and Environment Canada.
We have offered our considerable expertise to that province, and Quebec Hydro has taken advantage of that offer not only in respect to Phase I studies, which I have summarized in my preceding remarks, but also in respect to Phase II, in which we will be gathering a lot of new basic data necessary to carry out a thorough environmental appraisal.
If I could return to that point of principle which I tried to outline at the beginning of my remarks, Mr. Speaker, ecological investigations must precede the decision to uproot nature, to uproot our natural surroundings. In other words, Mr. Speaker, environmental engineering must be completed before construction starts on a large scale. This is a principle which I believe the province of
April 28, 1972

Quebec endorses, or certainly appears to endorse, in respect to the Janies Bay development. It is certainly one in which this government believes wholeheartedly.

Hydro, or in recent times occasionally Manitoba Hydro, and now Quebec Hydro. They seem to find that the biggest villians in this piece are government-owned Crown corporations.

This has been true of British Columbia Hydro in recent years and also of Manitoba Hydro. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am really quite pleased to participate in this debate in view of the fact that all hon. members have recognized the importance of this project for the province of Quebec and the fact that it is closely related to the interests of the country.
I want to make a few comments on what has already been said as well as on the project itself; it is my duty as a member representing a Quebec riding. Above everything else, I would like to ask all hon. members to deal with the matter as objectively and impartially as possible.
We all know that this project, the cost of which has been estimated at $6 billion and which should provide jobs for 125,000 workers, is of vital importance to the province of Quebec in the present context.
All hon. members will recognize that if the province of Quebec could improve its economic situation by means of that project, the whole of Canada would profit by it.
I listened with pleasure to the speeches of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald), of the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis) and of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) who successively showed clearly that the initiative proposed by the mover of this motion (Mr. Aiken) was not as necessary as the motion made it out to be. The Minister of the Environment and the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development told us that negotiations have been going on for some time with the province of Quebec, which I readily approve.
I should like at the outset of my remarks to ask the federal government to comply with the Quebec government's request, as regards the services as well as the facilities the federal government can provide for the carrying out of that project.
Although the project is typically a Quebec one, I do not believe the Quebec government should be left to carry it
1744

I am confident that these basic principles will not be overlooked by any member of this House.
Mr. Speaker, before concluding my remarks, I should like to quote from what was said by a university professor about James Bay. His lecture was entitled, Can the Province of Quebec afford to do without this project? I quote:
Considering the number and complexity of the tasks which await us, considering the huge sums of money-billions of dollars-involved in the hydro-electric, industrial and human development of this territory, some people have asked whether Quebec could commit itself fully to this bold course, whether we can afford such a grandiose policy.
Of course, this will entail rather heavy expenditures. There is some concern over the control of investment in Canada, over the extent to which the federal government can appropriate money for this project. It should be well recognized that the government of Quebec is not that eager to borrow from the United States or elsewhere the money that will be needed.
Surely, the federal government should consider the possibility of making available to the province of Quebec financial assistance which would enable it to realize this project and that would be Canadian investment.
Instead of worrying about the fact that the government of Quebec is borrowing money abroad, some thought should be given from time to time to the assistance that could be offered by the federal government, not only to Quebec but to other provinces as well for projects of public interest. I quote again:
I suggest that this problem should be considered from another angle. Statistics showing the increasing number of people old enough to work indicate that if unemployment in Quebec is to be reduced from 8 per cent on the average in 1971 to 4.5 per cent as it was in 1966, jobs must be created for 75,000 newcomers on the labour market, for each year during the next ten years. In order to create one new job in industry or construction, an investment of $50,000 is needed today. If half the new jobs are to be opened in these two directly productive fields, as compared to jobs in the administrative and service fields, which in the end are supported by the two others, an investment of nearly $2 billion a year will have to be made for new activities in industry and construction.
The question should not be: "Can we afford to invest $1, $2, $3 or $4 billion a year in the James Bay development project?" but: "Can we allow ourselves not to do it, and what would the alternative be?"
Is it not really the aim which all hon. members should be seeking too? I leave it to them.
Mr. Speaker, I wanted to make these few comments in order to state that I was in favor of the James Bay development project, and especially to urge, in a very special way, the federal government to co-operate willingly, as far as possible, as the responsible ministers have done it. Therefore, I urge them to continue in the same direction, and as a member from a riding which is located in the province involved, I take the liberty to urge all other members from other provinces to co-operate to the realization of this project, not only for the benefit of Quebec but for the benefit of Canada as a whole. They can count, from now on, on my co-operation and that of all Quebec members, as if it were a project introduced by another province and in which the interest of the whole country was at stake.

In any event, the motion which has been brought before the House is of interest. I think the debate has been largely academic, because whatever we say here will not make the slightest difference to the direction the government is taking or to the direction the government of Quebec is taking. It will not make the slightest difference to the claims of the Indian people to which I intend largely to confine my remarks. I say this because the project is going ahead. Roads and bridges are already under construction. Some are almost completed. We are told by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development that negotiations are being conducted. But there does not seem to be very much sense in conducting negotiations for the return of a cow after the animal has been killed and eaten.
The Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis) says that ecological studies are being carried out. But surely, to be useful, these studies ought to have been made long before the project was ever started. With respect to the treatment of these studies by the Indian people themselves, the report to which the minister referred at some length was actually burned, together with a great many other reports, by the people at Ruperts House late in February shortly after release for publication. The minister quoted at length from the study of December, and one of the recommendations contained in it, in addition to those he read, appear in a report which was printed in the Montreal Star of February 24.1 quote:
An element in the book burning is that the people resent a statement in the ecology report-a perfunctory, throw-away statement-that people here depend on white people and that do not depend on trapping and hunting "as much as some people think."
If this is a gauge of the calibre of the study being conducted by both governments, and which the minister cites as his authority for saying that this ecological survey is being carried out, if this is a measure of the concern felt for the rights of the native people affected by this project, then I suggest the report is not of much use, anyway.
The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has chosen to make a great distinction between representations which he receives officially and representations which he receives otherwise. He continually makes this distinction. He is resting his oars on it now. The native brotherhoods which have been set up across the country

are being used by the minister as a political buffer between the actions of his department and the legitimate requests of the native people. I would remind him that he has responsibility under the Indian Act to consider not only the representations of provincial and territorial brotherhoods; he has a duty to consider the representations made to him by individual band councils, indeed, by individual Indians in this country. So when he stands in his place and sheds crocodile tears because he has not received any representations of an official nature, I do not feel much sympathy for him. Indeed, I condemn him for abdicating his responsibility under the Indian Act to do something positive.
I ask the minister this: What is the use of standing in this House today and telling us he has refrained from intervening in this affair because of a fear of being paternalistic, because he has been asked by the Quebec Association of Indians to wait until they call him, when all the time the project is moving inexorably ahead? Granted, the minister may not have received representations from the Quebec brotherhood, officially, until last Monday, but he cannot say he was not aware of the problems which are confronting these people, that he was not aware of their concern for their rights in the land which is affected by this project. Nor can he tell us he is not charged directly with responsibility, as minister, to intervene to ensure that the legal rights of the Indians in

this area, founded upon the documentation which has been read into the record by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett), are protected.
The minister tells us, in his holier-than-thou attitude, that we should not use these people as a political football, thus hoping to excuse his inaction in discharging his responsibilities towards them. He says he hopes members will not take extreme positions. But I suggest to him it is not playing politics to direct criticism at him and his department where criticism is justly deserved, and it is not taking an extreme position to criticize the minister for failing to discharge his responsibilities as clearly set forth in the documents already placed on record and in the Indian Act. It does not do very much good for the Indian people, whose land rights are affected, for the mininster to "snow" the House with platitudes about not wanting to be paternalistic to the native people affected and not wanting to intervene. These people had the right to expect his help, and to expect his intervention, to protect their rights from the very outset, but they did not get it. In this regard, the minister has absolutely abdicated his responsibilities under the act.
What good, I ask, will holding a meeting with the government of the province of Quebec do now? What good will it do now that the authority has already been granted for the project to proceed? What good will it do in areas affected by construction of roads and bridges already under way over lands to which these people have a legal right? His duty was to do something before the authority was granted to get the project under way. His clear duty under the act was to do something before the project, or any part of it, got under way. His clear duty under the act was to ensure that the rights of these people were secured and that their bargaining position would thereby be secured. Their bargaining position at the moment, and in any negotiations that follow, have to be seriously weakened by his inaction.
These people cannot now say, "Retain for us some of these traditional hunting and fishing rights from which we and our ancestors have made our living for over 100 years". All they can say now is: "You have taken away our land rights, overrun our lands; you are going to destroy our traditional hunting and fishing grounds and take away our lands from us from which we have gained our livelihood for centuries; we therefore need compensation". All they can negotiate for now is compensation, and that from a very weak position because of the inaction of the minister and his abandonment of his clear duty under the Indian Act.
The combined chiefs who sent the minister the petition should have been heard. The minister spoke recently in committee about this great dialogue that is going on between him and his departmental officials respecting the formulation of policies affecting the native people of Canada. It is dialogue that is one way, dialogue that the minister and the government of which he is a part construe as meaning the setting and the formulation of unilateral policies, policies formed without consultation with the Indian people, as clearly substantiated by the report of the subcommittee of the cabinet considering the funding of native associations which was submitted to the

That information comes from individuals on the spot. I might also inform the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis) that I am told that none of the areas that it is intended to flood by the dams and rivers to be constructed in this project are going to be denuded of timber, of growing trees. This will effectively destroy a good deal of the viability of the land so far as it has the capacity to support the needs of the Indian people of the area.
With respect to the minister's defence of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) concerning the applications made under the Navigable Waters Protection Act for construction of bridges, again it is my understanding that the bridge at Mattagami was two-thirds completed before any application was made for permission to build it, and before federal approval was obtained. The only hope that the Indian people who are affected by this project have at this stage, now that they have been sold down the river, as it were, by the minister, is to negotiate for some form of compensation. What can be negotiated? In my view, the only negotiations possible are in the area of the establishment of an industry that will replace that which has been taken from them, namely the way they have made their living in the past. I suggest, perhaps, their participation in industries such as tourism, fish and duck camps, perhaps in boatbuilding, woodworking, canoe making. It will not be much good to come up with a settlement involving dollars that they will put in the bank; that will not keep the Indian people of the area alive.
The action of the minister, or rather his lack of action in my view, in this matter has been deplorable. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) and the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development have bobbed, ducked and weaved all over the place on this question. It is only now that the resolution of the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) is before the House that they have come up with some examples. I am really surprised by this. I am really surprised that he or some member of the government has not come to the House and

I thank hon. members for their courtesy, Mr. Speaker. The other serious aspect-I will be brief-is the conflict of interest with which the minister is confronted here. He is the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and as such he has direct responsibility to care for the best interests of the people coming under his jurisdiction, namely, the Indian and Eskimo people of Canada.
On March 15, as reported in a Montreal newspaper, he approved of the James Bay project. I do not have the

April 28, 1972
James Bay Power Project
quotation immediately available, but he did approve of the James Bay project on that date. Shortly thereafter he said in the House of Commons that he did not morally approve of the project. I will read that quotation in a moment. On March 29 the minister stated in the House, as recorded at page 1265 of Hansard for that date:
Mr. Speaker, I have no moral approval to give on this proposal. I repeat once again that I follow very carefully the talks taking place between the Indians and the Quebec government on the James Bay proposal. In due course, at the Indians' request, I shall be glad to participate in the discussions.
Not only is there a conflict between his statement of March 15 in Montreal and this statement, but he said again on April 24 that he did not have to establish Indian priorities in Quebec. It is his clear responsibility to do so, yet he is telling members of the House that he has no such responsibility. As a minister of the Crown he is coming down on the side of approval of this project, yet at the same time he has a responsibility to take action under the Indian Act to maintain the integrity and security of the rights of these Indian people. These are the rights of the people involved in the James Bay project. So there is here a clear conflict of interest.
I am not alone in this view. This opinion has been expressed in the press and by others concerned with Indian affairs. It seems to me the government is confronted, in respect of this project, with a clear requirement to decide whether the Minister of Indian Affairs should continue to act while the government is taking a stand to approve a project which is directly to the disadvantage of the Indian people involved.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take up too much time in this very interesting debate. I commend the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) for raising the topic. I am tempted in some ways to perhaps take out my tomahawk on this issue, but I will save that for later.
When speaking on this question I suppose it could be said that if the Indian people had adopted a different immigration policy many of these problems would not have arisen. On the other hand, I am reminded of my good friend Gus Gottfriedsen, chief of the Kamloops band. The reservation there is across the river from Kamloops, and when he looks across the river he says, "I see the white men building cement basements. I guess they intend to stay here for a while."
This topic has been a very lively one in all parts of the country, especially in my constituency. I suppose there are a number of reasons for that. There is a very large Indian population in the province of British Columbia, 50,000 or so, and there are 12 or more reservations in my constituency. We have been faced in the Kamloops-Cariboo area with a situation which involves similar principles. There was an attempt some years ago to divert water from the Shuswap River to the Okanagan River. It was being made on very narrow grounds-actually, on a purely physical basis. In a report by the provincial government it was stated that it was physically possible to move water from point A to point B. The government did not consider any of the environmental consequences.
I understood from the remarks of the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis) that he feels it is regrettable that

many of the projects developed in the past were carried out without consideration of the total environmental picture, the environmental consequences and what might happen if you divert water, in this instance, from the Shuswap River to the Okanagan River. The members of various governments which made these decisions did not consider what might happen if you dam a river or a series of rivers. They did not consider the ecological consequences.
I am pleased that the people in my constituency, particularly those in the Kamloops-Shuswap area, got up on their hind legs and fought very hard against the proposal to divert water from the Shuswap River into the Okanagan River. As a result of the fight they put up, we were able to obtain what is called the Okanagan basin water agreement, signed by the province of British Columbia and the federal government. The resulting study will be one of the most comprehensive, in respect of water, ever carried out in this country. I think this is the best way to proceed in respect of such a project.
Environmental and ecological consequences must be evaluated before decisions are made. I regret that in the case of the James Bay project the ecological and environmental parameters were not investigated before the decision was made. That is very regrettable. As we go down the trail from here I hope that with a very enlightened Minister of the Environment, a very enlightened parliament and Department of the Environment situations such as this will not occur. I hope we will be much better informed about our environment and ecology, which involves birds, bees and animals of all kinds, before this type of decision is made.
Let me deal for a moment with the report on the James Bay project, entitled "A preliminary study of the environmental impacts of the James Bay development project".

I will get to that. I should like to quote a few paragraphs from this report which I think are significant and represent the kind of thinking that should take place before the project proceeds. The report reads in part:
Any intervention in the environment, if it modifies any one resource, agent or process, is bound to have an effect at every strata of the ecosystem, through the close interactions between resources, agents and processes. Prior to any intervention it is necessary to determine at least the orders of magnitude and significance of the impacts and to evaluate the relative vulnerability or compatibility of the site with respect to the anticipated development. In this context the terms "magnitude" and "significance" are not necessarily synonymous.
If the specialists' views and recommendations had been heeded, many of the environmental consequences of the Great Aswan High Dam-some of which have been described as disastrous- could have been avoided; but none of these specialists had "the strength or the influence to be heard at governmental or policy levels ... while the integrating forces of human society in Africa and elsewhere come apart in the face of single-tracked ramrod solutions that erode, then erase, our environment"
That is a significant statement. Another significant paragraph reads as follows:
If man is to become an intelligent resource manager, he will need to take the proper steps, indicated by ecologists and other
April 28, 1972

environmental specialists, to restore nature to a new state of equilibrium at least as diversified and productive as before.
I should like to turn to some of the conclusions outlined in this report which bother me very much. The first conclusion reads:
On the basis of limited data available, the Task Force can identify only one ecological impact of potentially alarming proportions and significance-the impact on the native population of the area. Appropriate action must be taken in advance to alleviate the ensuing disturbance in their mode of life.
It continues:
The hydroelectric development project will affect about 6,000 people (approximately 90% Indians), distributed along the coast and inland in the following settlements:
I will leave it at that, and quote from another paragraph with which I should like to take issue.
Indians in the area are, economically and politically, strongly dependent on white man's society. Fishing, hunting and trapping are still important social and economic activities in the life of the region, but the Indians are no longer as economically dependent on them as some people think.
I should like to challenge that statement. I disagree with it and I will deal with it a little more fully at some later date. I am going to be participating in the meetings when the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) meets the people of Quebec. I should like to examine all of the facts before I take out my tomahawk in this particular case.
There are three points I should like to make in the summation of my remarks. As I said before, it is regrettable that projects like this in James Bay commence without studies being made well ahead of the decisions. Decisions should be based on good, sound studies rather than trying to justify them by studies later. Second, it is my hope that a satisfactory solution to this problem can be worked out between the Indian people in the James Bay area and the government of the province of Quebec. I hope that as a result of these dealings with the province of Quebec, a new and better life can be found for these Indians, if this is their wish. However, it is imperative that they be adequately consulted and their wishes respected.

He has done a lot of things, taken some pretty hard decisions and has a very tough role. In many respects, the Minister of Indian Affairs is somewhat like the Minister of Finance. The people always say none of them is really good.

That is a lot of
baloney. It just is not the case. We have some very competent Indian leaders on the scene today who are supporting the rights of Indian people. In closing, I want to offer any assistance I can give to the people of Quebec and the people of James Bay. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to take part in this discussion. I have listened very carefully to the speeches made and I think I have learned something from them. maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POWER EFFECTS OF JAMES BAY HYDROELECTRIC PROJECT
