maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POWER EFFECTS OF JAMES BAY HYDROELECTRIC PROJECT
speechtext:
I thought that if the statement was affirmative it would be permissible. During the last election in the province of Quebec the idea was born of establishing 100,000 jobs for the people of the province. In looking for ways in which this might be accomplished, the decision was taken to start the James Bay power development

project. This was done in a totally political atmosphere. No study was undertaken by the provincial government. As a matter of fact, the project had not been discussed to any great extent.
You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that Mr. Kierans, an engineer from Sudbury, put forward the idea of developing the Grand Canal which was a diversion from Hudson Bay and which would have taken in the Rupert River, the Harricanaw River, the Moose River, probably the Mataga-mi River, the East Quebec River and a number of other rivers flowing into the James Bay area. This project was also supported federally by the Liberal government. One of the candidates in my area spoke about running barges up from Ottawa to New Liskeard. Freight was to be floated back and forth and industries would thus be established. Suddenly we found that the provincial government would receive the benefits.
Before the hon. member for Kamloops-Cariboo (Mr. Marchand) leaves, I would like to say that I am not very proud of the representation that he has made. He has been more interested in supporting the position of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) than in speaking for the people who need to be represented here. I know some of the Indian people in that area. They have been in the bush for years. They have been trapping and they have made a livelihood from that way of life. Their way of life, in my opinion, has not prepared them in any way to question the power of the Quebec government, which in any case does not brook questioning from anyone. They have not been able to speak for themselves. They have been in need of strong representation and they have looked to the government to protect their interests.
My colleagues have drawn attention to the legal requirements of the treaties. The Indians for many years have been protected by the federal government under agreement. When the government gave to Quebec jurisdiction over the land in that area, we retained certain land rights on behalf of the Indians. The Indians themselves are not capable of putting up the kind of fight that is necessary. Here I am not referring to the Caughnawaga reservation where the Indians have been dealing with the government for a long time, or to the Six Nations reserve in Brantford which has been dealing with the government for a long time. I am referring to the nomadic people in the area who have not had much to do with governments, and the little experiences they have had with white people have been bad.
The hon. member for Kamloops-Cariboo has the right and the ability to speak on behalf of the Indian people and in my opinion it is his obligation to speak for them. In my opinion he should have supported the position that has been taken by many other people in the province of Quebec, namely, that the rights of the Indians must be protected. This has not been done, and I condemn the minister for not doing it on behalf of the Indians. The very least that the federal government, in particular the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, could have done was provide a legal precedent by applying to the Supreme Court of Canada for a decision regarding the land rights of Indians and what would be a reasonable settlement.
April 28, 1972

During this summer a $60 million project for building roads in that area is going forward. Under no circumstances does Quebec own that land. Anybody else would be protected by expropriation rights and would have the right to go to court. But a man who has been living from trapping, a man who has been only peripherally involved with white people, has no such right. All that the Indians have received from the white people has been bad, such as alcohol, dealings with the Hudson's Bay Company, and so forth. The Indians' way of life has not enabled them to deal with white men and to oppose the Quebec government, which has given no consideration to their rights.
If the hon. member for Kamloops-Cariboo is to represent the Indian people, and it is his right and responsibility to do so because he has a greater advantage than the rest of us, he will have to say that the minister has not done a good job. Instead, he supports the minister. The project has already been started; the bulldozers and developers have moved in.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POWER EFFECTS OF JAMES BAY HYDROELECTRIC PROJECT
speechtext: Don't just pick on me.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POWER EFFECTS OF JAMES BAY HYDROELECTRIC PROJECT
speechtext:
I am not just picking on the hon. member. I, too, have an obligation toward the Indians because I represent five Indian reservations. All I am saying is that the hon. member is fortunate in having an advantage that I do not have. I am sure that because of his background he is able to go into these areas and talk to people who would resent my doing so. He is able to talk to the Indians who would violently resent the minister. They do not resent the hon. member because of his special birthright. Therefore, I say he has the obligation, and certainly the ability and the right, to act in a special way to ensure that those rights are not negotiated away.
The Indians' rights must be protected in a special way. That is why the Queen said she had a responsibility toward the people living on these lands. Just because it is the province of Quebec that is involved does not give this government the right to waive the treaties which give the Indians special rights. These are God-given rights until they themselves ask that they be revoked or modified.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POWER EFFECTS OF JAMES BAY HYDROELECTRIC PROJECT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POWER EFFECTS OF JAMES BAY HYDROELECTRIC PROJECT

An article in the Montreal Star of March 27 reads as follows:
The province began negotiating when a commission of inquiry under Judge Henri Dorion established that the native people have "real and incontestable territorial rights" over huge tracts of northern Quebec, including the James Bay area.
The provincial government, in what the association lawyers describe as a "sign of good faith", has already agreed-
It goes on to say that they waived the 8 per cent sales tax in the area. Big deal! They did say that they gave some concessions, but what are they to these 7,000 people who are not represented by any really unified force? To be fair to the minister I should point out that he has done a good job in helping the Indians to develop the ability to participate in meetings and to discuss their problems. This minister should be given full credit for that, but I suggest that he knows as well as I do that the Indians have not yet fully developed this ability.
James Bay Power Project
Four years ago the minister set up a meeting in Sudbury at which the chiefs sat around the table. Each one said, "I will pass because I want to hear what everybody else has to say". So 25 chiefs sat around the table and no one said anything until they came back to the first one who spoke. They all decided to wait until someone else had spoken, and no one got around to speaking. The people did not understand. The chiefs of the bands had never talked to each other before.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POWER EFFECTS OF JAMES BAY HYDROELECTRIC PROJECT
speechtext: That was four years ago.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POWER EFFECTS OF JAMES BAY HYDROELECTRIC PROJECT
speechtext:
That is right, and I give the minister full credit for having developed this policy. But it took us 200 or 300 years to do that. Now, how can we suddenly expect the Indians to stand on their own feet in our councils without our backing? The minister should not wait until they come to ask him. He is supposed to protect their interests. If he and his department leave it up to the Bourassa government, which is only interested in creating jobs for Quebec voters, the Indians will have nothing left to negotiate in a few years.
The Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis) today took another tack. He indicated he was very concerned that the department had not been able to ascertain a number of things that should be ascertained in advance of construction. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) showed a great weakness in his argument when he said we have not really discussed hydroelectric power as an energy resource, and that we do not know what our actual needs are. If we develop the power at James Bay, we may find that the province of Quebec cannot afford to make a $10 billion expenditure in that field, because power may be generated more cheaply through other means. I well remember an argument which took place in Saskatchewan a number of years ago, when it was pointed out that hydro power in that province was not the cheapest form of power, and that power could be produced more cheaply there through the use of thermo plants.
The Minister of the Environment indicated that his department had completed only a preliminary study, and the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development showed a great weakness in his ability to negotiate for the Indian people. I point out that these Indians are not like those in Fort George, Prince Rupert or any of the reserves. They live spread out over the entire area. I am sure many of them only know who their band chief is, and quite often that is the only relationship they have with their band. Some of them live permanently on reserves, but a very large number of them spend most of their time hunting and travelling around the territory in which their hunting grounds are traditionally located.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POWER EFFECTS OF JAMES BAY HYDROELECTRIC PROJECT
speechtext: And secured for them.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POWER EFFECTS OF JAMES BAY HYDROELECTRIC PROJECT

Yes, and secured for them. Despite what this House has been told, they are not in a position to negotiate. They will have to be protected by do-gooders. The James Bay Committee met in Montreal in March of this year. Most of the members of that committee are do-gooders. They have pointed out some very interesting things

concerning the attitude of the developers of the area. I quote from their report as follows:
The Development Corporation has gone ahead and started the construction of a road network without first seeking or obtaining the permission of the native peoples who live on the land. This contradicts public statements of the Corporation proclaiming concern about them.
The premise there was:
The inhabitants of the area will be the first to benefit from its development.

The program-as proposed-has to be enacted now.
The program will be enacted in any event. You can't stop progress.
The program is needed to fill the demand that will be created by the program.
No one opposes the program. It will benefit the majority, and harm no one.
Data used to estimate effects of the program are the only valid, pertinent data available.

All applicable alternatives have been considered.
That is the attitude of the developers. Obviously, that is the attitude of the Quebec government. You know, Mr. Speaker, the Quebec government was embarrassed by the Hamilton Falls project in Labrador. This did a great deal to hurt their prestige. They did not like it one little bit. Now, they think they have to do something to counteract that.
I plead with the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. I consider him to be a very progressive minister. He is a person who has thought out some of the problems of the Indians. This is something I do not say about his department. Some of the officials are as archaic as some of the treaties they are abusing. In my opinion, the minister is progressive but his departmental people are not. They are cowards. They won't really make any decision on anything that might get them into trouble or make work for them.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POWER EFFECTS OF JAMES BAY HYDROELECTRIC PROJECT
speechtext: You are just saying that because the minister used to be a member of the NDP.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POWER EFFECTS OF JAMES BAY HYDROELECTRIC PROJECT
speechtext:
I didn't know that. Well, there is a saving grace in everyone. I suggest that the minister should not rest on his laurels, on his ability to provide a new environment in which the Indian population will be able to negotiate. I ask the minister to give serious consideration to the claims of the Indian people to the territorial lands given to them by treaty. I consider those treaties to be sacred, held 
in trust by the federal government, not to be negotiated with provinces, not to be negotiated with developers but only to be negotiated with the Indian people.
We have a law in this country which provides that if people are not competent to enter into a legal agreement, then a legal agreement cannot be negotiated. It is my opinion that the Indian people are not competent to assess the value of what they possess. The native peoples are looking at their land in terms of their livelihood, in terms of their background, in terms of the use to which they put it. This is land that may be worth far more than any other type of land in 50 years time. Water may become our richest resource on this continent. It is something that, in its pure form, will be very precious. If this minister allows the Indians, in their ignorance of the potential of the land, in their inability to deal with the courts of the land, to lose their land, he will have failed in his duty. If he gives up the duty that has been entrusted to him by the people of Canada, and by the parliament of Canada, to protect this land which has been left as a heritage for the Indians by the Queen who negotiated the treaties in good faith, then he will have done nothing for democracy, nothing for the native peoples of this country, and he will be forever remembered as the one who sold out their heritage for a mess of potage.
The minister is a young man. I am sure he will be here for quite some time.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POWER EFFECTS OF JAMES BAY HYDROELECTRIC PROJECT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POWER EFFECTS OF JAMES BAY HYDROELECTRIC PROJECT
speechtext: But not as a minister.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POWER EFFECTS OF JAMES BAY HYDROELECTRIC PROJECT
speechtext:
I hope he is around for a long time, but I do not want him sitting in this House in two or three years time, and saying to himself and the people of Canada that if he had to do it over again he would do what he was supposed to do in the first place, that he would provide the protection to the Indian people that it was his obligation to provide, that he would provide it whether they asked for it or not, that he would make money available to them to protect their rights, rights which another government would have stolen from them because of their ignorance and because of his unwillingness to defend them.
Mr. Speaker, I may be unfair to the nature of the Indian people, but in my part of the country many of them are like children when it comes to dealing with the white man's problems. We have seen them in the courts, we have seen them trying to buy cars, we have seen them dealing in the white man's society in a less than competent manner. Knowing that, I cannot stand here and say that the minister should wait until they all get together and decide to come to him for protection. Mr. Speaker, he has an obligation to protect the Indian population in the James Bay area now. Anything less will be a sell-out of the rights which those Indians deserve in a fair and just society.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ian Watson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POWER EFFECTS OF JAMES BAY HYDROELECTRIC PROJECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to join other members of this House in expressing gratitude to the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) for affording us this opportunity to discuss a most impor-
April 28, 1972

tant question and one with which we are all likely to become more and more concerned during the next year or two.

When the Quebec Prime Minister introduced in the National Assembly Bill 50 on the development of the James Bay area, the main argument used by his opponents-the technocrats of the Parti Quebecois and of Quebec Hydro who led the opposition against Bill 50 in the National Assembly-was that it would be more profitable for Quebec to develop atomic energy than the hydroelectric potential of the James Bay area.
Given the increasing cost of building and maintaining atomic plants and the problem of controlling the pollution which those plants might cause, I believe that economically the hydroelectric project is to be prefered to atomic plants because of the touristic and mining advantages which will result from this project.
However, I was most concerned to find that during the debate on Bill 50 no mention was made of the Cree people who are the only residents in the area involved. Mr. Speaker, I would like now to deal with this subject.

Mr. Speaker, under certain circumstances I am convinced that this project could benefit the people of the area. In theory, it can supply jobs that the growing population along the coast of James Bay and the interior need. Until recently, wildlife resources in the area were adequate to provide a livelihood but this is no longer true.
When I was chairman of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development I visited the James Bay and Hudson Bay areas in the autumn of 1970 along with three other members of the committee. Meetings were held with the Cree peoples at Miskassini Post, East Main and Fort George and many things were discussed. The question of language seemed to bother the local people more than anything else. We put forward the proposition that the children learn both English and French in school, asserting that jobs in the hydroelectric industry or the mining industry would require a knowledge of French whereas the tourist industry and the prospecting industry would require English. They indicated that they would be interested in learning both languages but were insistent on their right to choose the language of instruction for their children. It should be remembered that the language of all these people at home and at work is still Cree.
In our discussions, the prospect of hydro development did not invoke any adverse reaction from the public audience. About a year later the project was officially announced and no doubt there will be additional reaction as more and more activity appears on the scene. In theory at least, in this kind of scheme we should be able to provide the type of development where the people would play a major role. However, judging by past experience, can we really hope that the Cree peoples of the James Bay region will have an important role to play? Certainly there is nothing in our recent history to justify that hope.
The Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development recommended that the education branch of the department should tackle innovative educa-
James Bay Power Project
tion for young Indians in the James Bay area because of the additional language problem there which is not faced by Indians elsewhere in Canada. The Department of Natural Resources of the province of Quebec wishes to have French as the working language of the area. This conflicts with the Anglican heritage of the Cree peoples, whose language remains basically Cree but whose exposure through religion has been to English, so there is some prejudice in favour of English rather than French.
Given this conflict of interest, the committee recommended that the department devote its initial energies to the inauguration of new teaching methods that would enable the younger people in the region to master both the English and French languages. That is asking a lot, considering that we in the rest of Canada are not able to do this. So far as I know, the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has not moved toward implementation of this particular recommendation.
We also urged, in our education committee report, a new approach to vocational training. One of the deficiencies in vocational training, whether in Indian schools or white schools in northern Canada, is that vocational courses supplied to youngsters and students simply do not reflect the industrial needs of the area. For instance, mining courses are not available where mines exist. We feel it is only common sense for the kinds of courses offered to students to reflect the kind of job opportunities that are likely to be offered in the area.
I am not aware yet of any innovation in our program which would permit, in the James Bay area and Hudson Bay areas, Cree youngsters to acquire the type of education and, later, the type of vocational education which is necessary if they are to play an important role in the hydroelectric developments projected there. If, on the other hand, everything that should be done were to be done, if we were to do everything to permit the Cree peoples of this area to play the major role which should be theirs in any hydroelectric development after the construction period is over, I am confident that the support of the indigenous peoples for this project would be increased. If that support were not guaranteed, at least there is a very high likelihood that the project would be approved by the Indian peoples living in the area.
Quebec, in its approach to the peoples of the area through the provincial department of natural resources, has not given us too much ground for encouragement.

The Minister of Natural Resources of Quebec has made the mistakes of paternalistic actions in New Quebec as our federal ministers responsible for the Indians have been making since the beginning of the twentieth century.

We are making the same mistakes all over again. Quite frankly, since the announcement of the James Bay project there has been nothing in the approach of the department of natural resources of the province of Quebec which would indicate a change of heart or a more enlightened approach to the job. There is nothing to show that any-

thing more has been done to prepare the indigenous peoples for the new kind of development which is proposed.
It is all very well to talk about settling with our Indian peoples in the area and negotiating with them. Whether these negotiations succeed or not, I am convinced that the Indian peoples could decide on legal measures which would effectively block the project for years. I would say to Premier Bourassa that this is a very real possibility. The Indian peoples of these areas are not simple people who have recently come out of the woods and who are unaware of the ways of the white man. I could name Chief Diamond of Rupert House and Chief Kanatewat of Fort George as two extremely capable and competent chiefs. If they are at all representative of the calibre of the chiefs of this area, those people will adopt a very energetic and hard position on whatever is being negotiated.
I am confident that with the advice of legal people now assisting them, and their lawyers are among the best in the country, the chiefs will adopt the kind of legal position that will protect their peoples now and in the future. I therefore warn the minister and the authorities in Quebec responsible for this project that the possibility of legal measures holding up operations in the James Bay area in the next year or two are very great. Indeed, this is likely.
Putting aside for the moment legalities and the question of whether legal positions will be adopted, I submit that there is little evidence to show that the kind of enlightened approach that is necessary if the peoples of the area are to be brought into the modern world is being adopted in the circumstances. These new approaches are not evident and they ought to be evident, Mr. Speaker.
For the past few minutes I have dealt with Indian affairs. Now, I wish to touch briefly on other aspects of the project. The Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis) indicated that environmental impact statements are now being insisted on in connection with major projects in this country and elsewhere in the world. Such environmental impact statements would involve the work of top biologists, laboratory people, forestry people, meteorologists, climatologists, etc. I wonder-I admit that perhaps I did not hear the minister referring to this subject matter and that there may have been a reference to it-whether there is any plan to produce scale models of this entire project, either in some computerized form or physically, in order that we may determine clearly and without doubt that in the long run this project will not adversely affect climate, the ecology of the rivers and James Bay and Hudson Bay in a way that will have far reaching effects on the continent and even, perhaps, on the world.
Another fear I harbour has been stimulated somewhat by a paper I received from a local STOP group-Society to Overcome Pollution-of my riding. This group, under the chairmanship of Mrs. Evelyn Retallack, prepared an excellent study of the James Bay project and was kind enough to let me have a copy of it. While I do not agree with everything in the report, it does contain one subject that no other speaker today has covered. The warning in that particular part of the report warrants further study by the department headed by the Minister of the Environment. Mr. Sylvestre, formerly with the department of lands and forests of Quebec, has warned that in the area south of James Bay there is a potential earthquake and

landslide zone. Montreal, he says, is located on a fault running along the St. Lawrence River. He goes on to point out that the Canadian Underwriters Association now has refused to give automatic earthquake insurance to people in the Montreal area. Man and His World was specifically refused earthquake insurance. Mr. Sylvestre goes on to say:
The 50,000 square miles to be flooded and the billions of tons of water in new weight this land must bear, presents very strong dangers for the residents of all of North America south of the project.
Oxford geographer Gordon Rattray Taylor in his book "Doomsday Book" deeply explores the correlation between seemingly natural catastrophes and man, the engineer, as earthquake maker. Pressure changes are known to shift the crust of the earth causing earthquakes in the process. Through intensive scientific and technical research, such earthquakes as the one in India in 1967 and the one in Rhodesia in 1963 can be traced to the filling of the reservoirs created by the Koyna Dam in India and the Kariba Dam in Rhodesia. These areas were quite free of shocks before the dams were built. The dam at Monteynard in the French Alps cause a series of tremors culminating in a shock of several points on the Richter scale. The artificial lake of Kremasta in Greece caused earth slides and fractures-480 homes collapsed and 1,200 were seriously damaged.
The possibility that man might be disturbing the earth's crustal forces only dawned on scientists in 1945 when Dr. Carder pointed out what was happening at Boulder Dam, Colorado. There had been no shocks in this area for 15 years before the dam was built. Lake Mead, formed by the dam, began to fill in 1935. The first shock came in 1936. During 1937 more than 100 shocks were felt. When the lake reached its full depth the shocks reached a maximum with further bursts in several years when the lake was particularly full.
In view of this it has been suggested that the disastrous earthquake which hit Iran and Turkey in 1957 and in 1966 were caused by changes in the level of the Caspian Sea. The water level had fallen six feet as a result of the industrialization of the lower Volga Valley.
He goes on to mention the slides in the St. Jean-Vianney area in Quebec. I think the point is fairly made that the addition of this extra weight caused by billions of tons of water on a 50,000-square mile area, an earthquake-prone area, might quite conceivably have a disastrous result. It may well be that as a result of geological and other research it will be determined that the structure along the St. Lawrence River bears no relation to that around James Bay and that land pressures there could not conceivably affect the St. Lawrence valley. But no word of such a finding has come from the minister, and I would suggest that at least this is an essential question for study in connection with our environmental approach to this project.

A further point which I feel should be mentioned is this: at some stage the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) should indicate the effects on the national economy of attempting to handle the James Bay project and the two Mackenzie pipelines for gas and oil, from the point of view of the almost intolerable pressure which will be placed upon the Canadian dollar. Undoubtedly if this were the result, Canadian ability to compete in world trade would be seriously impaired.
Even if there is an assurance forthcoming that in the long run the ecological effects of this project will be minimal, that no serious danger of earthquakes will be involved and that the financing will not throw our economy out of balance, and leaving aside the legal aspects of the Indian peoples' position, we will still be left with the special problem of ensuring that the indigenous peoples of this area receive a decent deal. I am thinking in terms of a deal which will enable them to face the future not only with confidence but with competence, the competence which an adequate system of education could give them and which is not being given them now. An enlightened approach must be forthcoming from the education branch of the federal Department of Indian Affairs, the department of natural resources and the department of education in Quebec.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the hon. member for Parry Sound-Mus-koka (Mr. Aiken) for using this rule relating to emergency debates intelligently, perhaps for the first time in my memory; and you, Mr. Speaker, for recognizing that fact. Many phony efforts have been made to use this rule and at last the hon. gentleman has come up with an intelligent one. I wish him well.
When this issue came to the fore in February, parliament was not in session but a press release was issued dealing with a joint federal-provincial report on the environmental impact of the project. That report dramatically illustrated the inadequacy of Canadian procedures for handling environmental problems.
I intend to focus my remarks on the final points made by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka. I think the joint federal-provincial report made it clear that instead of a full evaluation of environmental damage and costs being made at the time the engineering and economic studies were carried out, the report was made after the decision to proceed with the James Bay development had been taken. Thus, it came too late to be of use in evaluating the project.
This is "cart before the horse" decision-making. I think it is the wrong way to go about major developments involving an alteration in the environment. Instead, there should have been studies made of all the factors involved, economic, engineering, social and environmental before proceeding to any decision as to whether construction should begin. Only in this way can a proposal such as the James Bay project be properly evaluated.
I should like to refer to the situation created in connection with the Bennett dam in British Columbia, where costly remedial construction is now being undertaken to rectify the environmental problems ignored when the decision to build the dam was taken. The situation in
James Bay Power Project
James Bay might be compared to the situation which has now arisen in northern British Columbia. I would have thought that the Bennett dam would have been an object lesson on the dangers of this nineteenth century approach, but apparently the lesson has not been learned. What I would like to see instead of our present ramshackle, hit-or-miss procedures is something akin to the United States legislation, the environmental policy act of 1969 which despite its defects would make an excellent model for Canadian legislation. It is the model for a private member's bill of mine which I am sure the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka would be happy to second. I would present it to him with that in mind because I think it is a bi-partisan sort of approach.
What we should have is a systematic, interdisciplinary approach to these major engineering undertakings, one that will ensure that the natural and social sciences, environmental design arts and the planning and decision-making are properly integrated. We need a recommendation or a report on any major undertaking that might significantly affect the quality of the human environment, and a detailed study by the responsible federal or provincial, or joint federal and provincial, authorities should be made.
Such a report should include the environmental impact of proposed action. It should include any adverse environmental effects that cannot be avoided should the proposal be implemented. It should also include alternatives to the proposed action. It should include the relationship between local, short-term use of the environment and area and the maintenance, the enhancement as it were, of what you might call long-term productivity. Finally, it should include a statement on the irreversible and irretrievable commitment of resources that would be involved if the proposed action should be implemented. I realize that this sounds rather technical in form but I think hon. members are quite capable, without further elaboration, of understanding how it could be applied to the James Bay project and how, if such report had been prepared prior to any decision to proceed, we would have been a great deal better off than we are now.
It is my view that once such reports are prepared they should be made public and they should then be subjected to public scrutiny. Unfortunately, this House has not seen fit to re-establish what was an excellent committee of the House, the special committee on environmental pollution, on which the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Harding), the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka as well, I may say modestly, as myself did some excellent work. The House has not seen fit to re-establish that committee, a failure for which I think the government House leader is directly responsible. It is most unfortunate that he has taken this retrogressive step.
It is my view that with such a committee the members of this House would be able to examine projects such as this, report upon them and perhaps come up with a decent assessment of any damage that might be done, along the lines that I have suggested. We do not have any legislation such as the legislation I referred to, which is basically American. Neither, unfortunately and most regrettably, do we have the committee I have just mentioned. Therefore, I feel it is incumbent upon the Minister of the Envi-

ronment in particular to make sure that my private member's bill, which I earlier said would, I am sure, be supported by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka as well as the hon. member for Kootenay West, lays the foundation for his bringing forward soon some government legislation that will achieve these objectives and permit the making of environmental impact studies such as the one I have suggested, allow the publication of such statements and the holding of public hearings of interested parties who would be able to make their views known.
It is late on a Friday afternoon and I have no wish to prolong the debate. However, I hope that my plea, though
it falls on a rather thinly attended House, will not fall on deaf ears and that before long we will have procedures in this House as well as in legislation to allow us better to deal with the sort of problem we are faced with this afternoon.
